doc.title: Mike Vax interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 29, 2022

title: Kenton and the founding of jazz education
summary: Kenton's role in starting NAJE and the summer camps.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Yes. When you said that about putting personal expression into classical music it made me think of him because he did that. He could do that. Well this has just been a fascinating conversation, and I wonder, to wrap up, if you think back to when Stan and a few of the others sort of launched jazz education, could you envision what now in 2022, what the business of jazz education has arrived at? The state of it now?

You know it’s interesting, the original National Association of Jazz Educators, the original one, was basically Stan’s idea. And they were at I forget if it was Midwest or they were at one of the big conventions and the Kenton band had played. And I can tell you some of the guys that were there: Leon Breeden, Gene Hall, Jack Wheaton, Herb Wong, Matt Benton. They were in Stan’s suite and they were bemoaning about there’s no jazz at these conventions. There’s nothing going on what are we doing, and basically get off your butts and start something and get it going and what a lot of people don’t know is Stan put up the original money. He said, “We have to get this —” and Stan was, one of the things with the Kenton Legacy Orchestra that we say is we are not trying to be the Stan Kenton Orchestra, we are carrying on his tradition of jazz education and creative music. He believed that if jazz was going to survive you had to get to the young people. Because how else — forget more musicians, how are you going to have an audience? If young people aren’t being exposed to it how is there going to be an audience in another ten, fifteen, twenty years? You know? And so he really believed, and he was the first band leader to bring his band into schools on a regular basis, and from that Maynard did it and Woody did it and even Basie a little bit. But he was really the first one to get that going and of course with the national stage band camps which became the Kenton summer camps, Ken Morris was the administrator of those and had come to Stan and said, “I want to start summer jazz camps and I want you to be the resident band.” And Stan jumped at it immediately and so they formed, the first one was 1959. And then I went to the one in 1960 and it was at Indiana University. And of course it blossomed out into where they were doing five or six every summer. You know? And so I think that what has happened in schools, it’s sort of going backwards a little bit I’m sad to say but you know during the 60s and 70s, 60s it was getting started, 70s it got strong and 70s 80s, even into the 90s, it was really strong.
